246.title: A castle of crystal (Interior Castle, 1)
246.hook: the soul is a castle with many rooms and God at the center; the door is prayer
246.howItsDone: Many Catholics read Teresa of Ávila's Interior Castle slowly, often with a spiritual director or a prayer group, as a map of how a life of prayer grows from the first rooms toward the center.

segments.voice: Yesterday, unknowing: God is reached by love, not thought. Today, a new part of the path: one woman, one castle.

Spain, 1577. An aging nun with a head full of noise, she says, is ordered by her superiors to write a book about prayer. She doesn't want to. She has convents to run, letters to answer, a reform to hold together. She asks God what to write. And, as she tells it, while she is praying, a picture comes to her. The soul is a castle, made of diamond, or of very clear crystal. For the next eight days, this part of the path walks through it, room by room. Today, the front door.
screen: `SPAIN, 1577. A TIRED NUN.` → `ORDERED TO WRITE ABOUT PRAYER.` → `A PICTURE COMES TO HER.`

segments.voice: The nun is Teresa of Ávila, a Carmelite, later a saint and a Doctor of the Church. The book is The Interior Castle; in Spanish, Las Moradas, the dwelling places. First, the castle. It glows, clear as crystal, with many rooms, some above, some below, some to the sides. Teresa points to Jesus's own words, in the Douay-Rheims: "In my Father's house there are many mansions." If heaven has many rooms, she says, so does a human soul. Second, the center. In the very middle of the castle is the main room, and there God lives. Not far off in the sky. Inside. The soul's beauty, Teresa says, is so great you can hardly imagine it, and yet many souls never go in. They stay out in the courtyard. Third, the door. Her answer is simple: the door of the castle is prayer and reflection. Not a feeling. Not being good enough. Just turning toward God, even clumsily, even a little. Fourth, the first rooms. People who've just come in still carry a lot from outside, she says: worries, business, pride. She pictures snakes and other vermin slipping in with them, keeping them from seeing the light. The light from the center shines the whole time; they just can't see it yet. Her advice for these first rooms is humility: get to know yourself honestly, without panic. The castle has seven sets of rooms in all, taken one at a time.

segments.voice: Close your eyes and picture a clear, bright castle, with you standing just inside the door. Notice what came in with you, a worry, a grudge, a to-do list, without fighting it, then look toward the center, where the light comes from. If you pray, simply say, here I am; if you don't, rest in the picture of a light that was already on.

247.title: The second rooms
247.hook: struggle and backsliding; Teresa says keep going, don't turn back
247.howItsDone: Catholic spiritual directors often point people who have stopped praying to Teresa's second dwelling places and to her own story, encouraging a simple return to daily prayer without dwelling on guilt.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Interior Castle: God at the center, and the door is prayer. Today, the rooms just past the entrance, where it gets harder.

You start something good. A run every morning, a journal, a prayer before bed. The first week is great. The second week, the alarm goes off, it's cold, and a very reasonable voice in your head says: skip it, you're not really the type anyway. You skip three days, and the voice says: see? You've already failed. Might as well stop. Teresa of Ávila knew that voice well. She gives it its own set of rooms in her castle, and she has one piece of advice for anyone standing in them.
screen: `A GOOD START.` → `THE SECOND WEEK.` → `SEE? YOU ALREADY FAILED.`

segments.voice: First, who's here. The second rooms, Teresa says, belong to people who have begun to pray. They've stepped inside, and now they hear God calling them, through a good friend, a sermon, a book, even an illness or a hard season. That's the good news. The hard news: the pull of the old life hasn't gone anywhere. So these rooms, she says, can feel worse than the first ones. You hear the call, and you can't answer it well yet. Second, the voices. Teresa pictures the enemy of the soul whispering reasonable things: your friends will miss you, your health will suffer, other people seem fine without all this. The attacks are gentle, not dramatic. That's what makes them work. Third, falling. Teresa expects people here to fall, and doesn't pretend otherwise. Her advice: don't be discouraged, and don't stop praying. God can bring good even out of the fall. The real danger isn't slipping. It's deciding, after you slip, that you'll never go back in. Fourth, Teresa herself. In her autobiography she admits that as a young nun she gave up prayer for a long time, about a year, maybe more. She felt too unworthy to pray, and she thought that was humility. Later she called it one of the worst mistakes of her life. When she came back, she says, God was waiting. So when Teresa says keep going, she isn't lecturing from the top of a mountain. She's speaking from the second rooms, where she once turned around.
screen: `THE CALL YOU CAN'T YET ANSWER.` · `REASONABLE VOICES SAY GO BACK.` · `YOU WILL FALL. DON'T STOP.` · `TERESA ONCE STOPPED PRAYING.` · then, large: `JUST KEEP GOING.`

segments.voice: Think of something good you started and dropped: a habit of prayer, a walk, a call you used to make. Don't argue about why you stopped; just notice the gap. If you pray, come back the plainest way and tell God you're back, without a speech; if you don't, let these two minutes be your first step back into whatever you dropped.

Your line: just keep going. A fall is not the end of the road. Two hundred forty-seven days in.

248.title: The third rooms
248.hook: the well-ordered life that can still be a little too careful
248.howItsDone: Catholic retreat leaders often use Teresa's third dwelling places to help faithful, church-going people ask where their good habits have become too cautious, and what generous risk love might ask of them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, falling: you slip, and you don't turn back. Today, the rooms of people who are doing everything right.

Here's a certain kind of person. Up on time. Bills paid. Goes to Mass, gives to the collection, volunteers twice a year, never raises their voice. A good person, genuinely, with a life organized like a well-kept kitchen drawer. And yet sometimes, when something is asked that doesn't fit the drawer, a big risk, a messy person, a sudden need, they get very quiet and very reasonable. Teresa of Ávila built a whole set of rooms in her castle for these good, careful people. She's fond of them. And she's worried about them.
screen: `A GOOD, CAREFUL LIFE.` → `A WELL-KEPT DRAWER.` → `WHEN SOMETHING DOESN'T FIT.`

segments.voice: First, the praise. The people in the third rooms, Teresa says, have come a long way. They avoid sin, even small ones. They spend time in prayer. They're kind, they give, they keep their homes and lives in order. She calls this a real blessing, and she means it. Second, the young man. A rich young man comes to Jesus. He's kept every commandment since he was a boy. Jesus invites him to sell what he has, give to the poor, and follow. And, in the Douay-Rheims: "when the young man had heard this word, he went away sad: for he had great possessions." Teresa says he stays on her mind the whole time she writes about these rooms. Good all the way through, and then, at the one moment that asks for everything, a little too careful to let go. Third, the reason. Their love, she says, isn't yet strong enough to overwhelm their reason. Everything is sensible. Even their penances are as orderly as their lives. They worry about their health, their reputation, what could go wrong. And when a trial comes, they're surprised and hurt, because they've been so good. Fourth, the way on. Teresa's advice is humility, and a little daring. Stop measuring how far you've come. Don't wait until you can see the whole path before taking a step. Her worry, in a picture: a clean house is a good thing, but love sometimes means opening the door when someone knocks at a bad time. Tidy is good. Tidy is not the same as holy.

segments.voice: Ask where your life is a little too careful: a gift you keep meaning to give, a person you avoid because they're messy, a yes you keep postponing until things are calmer. 249.title: Two fountains (fourth rooms)
249.hook: one basin filled by pipes and effort, one filled from a spring beneath
249.howItsDone: In the Carmelite tradition, people who pray regularly are taught not to force feelings in prayer but to stay faithful and receptive, and spiritual directors use Teresa's two fountains to help them tell effort from gift.

segments.voice: Yesterday, possessions, and a young man who went away sad: tidy isn't holy. Today, halfway to the center, Teresa changes the picture to water.

Two stone basins sit side by side in a garden. Both end up full of water. But the first is fed by a long line of pipes and channels from somewhere far away. Somebody had to build all that, and somebody has to keep it working. You can hear the water clanking through. The second sits right on top of a spring. Nobody pipes anything in. It just fills, from underneath, quietly, and keeps on filling. Teresa of Ávila says prayer can come both of these ways. Today's word is the second one.
screen: `TWO BASINS IN A GARDEN.` → `ONE FED BY PIPES.` → `ONE SITS ON A SPRING.`

segments.voice: First, the pipes. The first basin, Teresa says, is like the good feelings that come from prayer by our own effort. We read, we think, we picture the Gospel scenes, we work at it. And it does bring joy; that's real, and it's good. But it comes the long way, with noise, through our own pipes. Second, the spring. In the second basin, the water rises from God, right at the source, and fills without anyone building anything. Teresa calls this the prayer of quiet. The mind may still wander, but the will, the deepest part that loves, is held still and at peace with God. The heart widens, she says, and she reaches for a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have run the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart." Third, you can't force it. Here Teresa is very clear. You can't dig for this spring, or make it happen by trying harder. It's a gift. What you can do, she says, is make room: be humble, keep praying, and don't cling to the feelings when they come or panic when they leave. Fourth, love over thinking. In these rooms she writes a line short enough to carry: the important thing isn't to think much, but to love much. If the mind is racing, let it, like a mill clattering in the background. The will can still rest by the spring. That's the difference between the two fountains. Not how much water. Where it comes from.
screen: `THE FIRST BASIN: OUR OWN EFFORT.` · `THE SECOND: A SPRING FROM GOD.` · `YOU CAN'T DIG FOR IT.` · `NOT TO THINK MUCH, BUT LOVE MUCH.` · then, large: `THOU DIDST ENLARGE MY HEART.`

segments.voice: Don't try to produce any thought or feeling; picture yourself as a basin, with the spring underneath. If you pray, stay with God without words, the way you'd sit beside someone you love without needing to talk; if you don't, let the stillness fill up on its own. When your mind clatters like a mill, let it clatter.
Quietud. Teresa's Spanish name for prayer that rises like a spring in the fourth rooms, a gift from God where the heart rests even as the mind wanders. Today's word.
Your line: the spring beneath. Some water can't be pumped, only received. See you in the fifth rooms.

250.title: The silkworm (fifth rooms)
250.hook: the worm spins its cocoon, dies, and a white butterfly comes out
250.howItsDone: Catholic teachers often use Teresa's silkworm to describe conversion as a slow dying to self and a new life in Christ, reached by prayer, the sacraments and conforming one's will to God's in daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two fountains and quietud: the spring beneath. Today, in the fifth rooms, Teresa reaches for something small and wriggling.

How silk is made. Teresa admits she has never seen it, only heard it told, and she tells it to her nuns anyway. A seed, tiny as a peppercorn, lies there as if dead. When the mulberry trees leaf out in spring, it wakes up as a little worm and starts to eat. And eat. It gets fat. Then one day it stops eating, and with its own mouth it spins silk around itself, thread by thread, until it's sealed inside a small house. Teresa marvels at it as one of the wonders of God's making.
screen: `A SEED LIKE A PEPPERCORN.` → `IT EATS, AND EATS.` → `IT SPINS ITSELF A HOUSE.`

segments.voice: First, the worm is the soul. Teresa says it begins like that seed, small and not doing much, until the warmth of God wakes it up. Then it feeds: on prayer, on the sacraments, on good books and sermons. It grows. Second, the cocoon. The house it spins, Teresa says, is Christ. She reaches for Saint Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "For you are dead; and your life is hid with Christ in God." The soul spins by what it does: prayer, letting go of self-will, small acts of love. God does the rest. Third, the dying. Inside the cocoon, the worm dies. That's the part that makes people wince, and Teresa doesn't soften it. The fat, busy, self-centered worm has to end. In these fifth rooms, she says, God draws the soul into a union so close that for a short time it's hardly aware of anything else, and then it comes out changed. Fourth, the butterfly. Out comes a little white butterfly, and Teresa is delighted by it. It's not the worm improved. It's something new. But she adds a surprise: the butterfly is restless. It doesn't know where to land anymore. The old things it used to crawl around on don't satisfy it, and it wants God more than ever. Teresa says that's not a problem. It's a sign. And she's honest that the change isn't always dramatic. There's a quieter road to this union too, she says: simply wanting what God wants, day after day. The butterfly can be born in an ordinary life.

251.title: The sixth rooms
251.hook: trials, longing, the ache of being close and not yet
251.howItsDone: In the Carmelite tradition, spiritual directors help people in seasons of trial and longing to read them as part of growing closeness to God, and Teresa's sixth dwelling places are often read slowly in such seasons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the silkworm: the cocoon, the dying, and the restless white butterfly. Today, that butterfly flies into the sixth rooms, where it aches.

The last night before someone comes home. Maybe they've been deployed, or away at school, or in a hospital two states over. The flight lands tomorrow. They're closer than they've been in months, and tonight is the hardest night of all. Sleep won't come. Every hour drags. The closeness is exactly what makes the waiting hurt. Teresa of Ávila says the sixth rooms of her castle are like that. She gives them more chapters than any other part of her book.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE THEY COME HOME.` → `CLOSER THAN EVER.` → `AND THE WAITING HURTS MORE.`

segments.voice: First, the trials. You might expect the rooms near the center to be all light. Teresa says no. Here the soul often meets hard things: people criticize or misunderstand, friends pull away, even praise becomes a burden, illness comes, and there can be times of inner darkness when prayer seems impossible. She lists them plainly, like someone who's lived every one. Second, the wound. God calls to the soul, she says, so quietly and so suddenly that it's like a spark, or a wound. It hurts, and it's sweet at the same time, and the soul wouldn't give up that pain for anything. It's the pain of love that knows its beloved is near and isn't fully here yet. Third, the longing. Everything in these rooms is longing. The soul is like the one in the psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God." A deer that has run a long way and smells water. Near enough to smell it. Not yet drinking. Fourth, Teresa's surprise. The longing isn't a sign that God is far away. It's a sign God is close. You don't ache for someone you've never met. The ache is what closeness feels like before it's complete. She adds a warning: extraordinary experiences can happen in these rooms, visions and words, but don't seek them, and judge everything by whether it leaves you more humble and more loving.
screen: `NEAR THE CENTER, HARD THINGS.` · `A CALL LIKE A SPARK, OR A WOUND.` · `A DEER THAT SMELLS WATER.` · `THE ACHE MEANS HE IS NEAR.` · then, large: `SO MY SOUL PANTETH AFTER THEE, O GOD.`

252.title: The seventh rooms
252.hook: at the center Martha and Mary work together
252.howItsDone: Catholic teachers point to Teresa's seventh dwelling places to show that the goal of contemplative prayer is not escape but love in action, and Carmelite communities join long hours of prayer with daily work and service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sitivit: the ache of being close and not yet, a sign that God is near. Today, at last, the center of the castle.

After a week of walking through rooms, you'd expect the center to be a throne room, or a cloud, or somewhere you never have to come back from. You'd expect the saint who reaches it to float off and stop doing laundry. Teresa of Ávila reached these rooms herself, she believed, and her life didn't float anywhere. She kept founding convents, riding in bumpy wagons, arguing with officials, writing letters about money and leaky roofs. She says that's exactly the point.
screen: `YOU'D EXPECT A THRONE ROOM.` → `TERESA KEPT RIDING IN WAGONS.` → `THAT'S THE POINT.`

segments.voice: First, the marriage. Teresa uses the language of love and marriage for the deepest union with God, following the Song of Songs and a long line of saints. In the sixth rooms the soul was betrothed. Here it's married, and the union doesn't come and go anymore. She gives two pictures. Two candles can be held together into one flame, then pulled apart. But rain falling into a river becomes the river. You can't find the raindrop again. Second, the peace. Trouble doesn't stop: there are still trials and noise around the edges of the castle. But in the center there's a stillness nothing reaches. Third, Martha and Mary. In Luke's Gospel, Martha rushes around serving while her sister Mary sits at Jesus's feet and listens. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful, and art troubled about many things: But one thing is necessary." People have used that story for centuries to rank prayer over work. Teresa won't. At the very center, she says, Martha and Mary must work together, so that the Lord is welcomed and fed. Fourth, the purpose. This is why all this prayer exists, Teresa says: to give birth to good works. Not feelings. Works. Look back at this week: a crystal castle with prayer as the door, the struggling second rooms, the careful third, two fountains, a silkworm, the long ache of the sixth. And at the center, not an escape from life, but a marriage that sends you back into it.
screen: `A RAINDROP FALLS INTO A RIVER.` · `STILLNESS AT THE CENTER.` · `MARTHA AND MARY, TOGETHER.` · `PRAYER GIVES BIRTH TO WORKS.` · then, large: `BUT ONE THING IS NECESSARY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next task waiting for you: an email, a meal, a shift, a chore. Sit with it a moment the way Mary sat, quiet, before you rise to do it the way Martha would. If you pray, offer the task to God before you begin; if you don't, choose who the work is for.
Spiritual marriage. Teresa's name for the union at the center of the castle, like rain falling into a river, which sends the soul back out to serve. Today's word.
Your line: martha and mary together. One listens, one serves, and both welcome the Lord. Day two hundred fifty-two, done.
